replies:
You don't have any Lincoln International application or interview recorded on file yet. The one step that starts that record is: tell me the interview date/time and paste (or summarize) the invite or the interviewers' names and roles so I can record it and make a tailored plan.

Prep now — short, high‑impact plan and mock questions for a final‑round analyst interview at Lincoln International:

1) What they’ll look for (one line)
- Technical accuracy in valuation/modeling, clear deal-story thinking (source → evaluate → structure), client-facing fit (communication, handling ambiguity, long hours) and attention to detail.
2) 30–minute prep plan (do this in order)
- 0–5 min: paste the invite or posting if you can; note sector focus and any skills they call out. If you can’t, assume generalist M&A/valuation focus.
- 5–20 min: refresh two technicals you will almost certainly be asked: LBO mechanics and a 3‑statement linkage / cash-flow bridge. For each, prepare a 3‑sentence answer and one quick numeric example you can speak aloud.
- LBO script: sources & uses → debt schedule → exit multiple / IRR drivers (leverage, multiple expansion, margin improvement, paydown). Example to say: “5x EBITDA buy, 4x exit after 4 years; with 2x debt/EBITDA initial and steady cash flow, IRR driven by deleveraging + small multiple uplift.”
- 3‑statement script: revenue → EBIT (margins) → NOPAT → addbacks (D&A) → working capital → capex → free cash flow → debt paydown. Say why EBITDA ≠ cash flow (capex and changes in WC).
- 20–30 min: prepare two short deal stories (STAR: Situation, Task, Action, Result) each 60–90 seconds and with a number:
- Story A (technical/modeling): a model you built or a case study—what you built, 2 key assumptions you tested, and the outcome or decision it influenced (percent change, valuation impact, time saved).
- Story B (client/team/pressure): a time you handled ambiguous feedback or tight deadlines—what you did, how you communicated, and the result.
- Optional: 30–60 min mock with me (I’ll ask questions and score).
3) Core answers to nail (one-liners + supporting detail)
- Tell me about yourself: 20–30 seconds—background, most relevant deal/project, and why Lincoln (boutique/breadth of deals or sector fit).
- Why M&A/why Lincoln: specific moment or project + what you enjoy (deal math + client influence).
- Walk me through your favorite model: state the model, your inputs, two key assumptions, sensitivity, and the business decision it supported.
- A time you disagreed with a teammate: situation, your action (data or alternative tested), and constructive outcome.
- Weakness/feedback: one real development area and what you did to improve with evidence.
4) Technical checklist to be able to say aloud (short definitions)
- DCF: WACC components, terminal value methods (perpetuity vs. exit multiple), and sensitivity tables.
- Comps vs. precedents: when to use each; precedents often show control premiums.
- LBO mechanics: sources & uses, debt schedule (interest, amortization), cash sweep vs. bullet, how leverage affects IRR.
- Accounting quick wins: depreciation → non-cash addback; capex and working capital moves cash.
5) How to handle modeling whiteboards / take-homes
- Narrate every assumption as you write it; anchor to a real comparable or market data if possible.
- Keep the math simple and check one key flow (revenue → EBIT → FCF) aloud.
- When stuck, state your assumption and why; offer to show sensitivity to that assumption.
6) Behavioral tips for final round
- Short, confident answers; lead with the headline (result or role) then backfill with 1–2 specifics.
- If asked about deals you didn’t lead, be explicit about your role and deliverable.
- Show commercial judgment: after a technical answer, add a one-line commercial implication or recommendation.
- Close fit questions by naming the sector/clients you’d enjoy working with at Lincoln.
7) 10-minute mock sequence I can run now (I’ll ask these in order)
- Walk me through a DCF you built — main steps and key assumptions you check.
- Explain an LBO and what drives IRR.
- Tell me about a technical modeling error you caught and fixed.
- Give a 60–90 second deal story showing your modeling impact.
- Why Lincoln International? (60 seconds)

If you want a mock now, I’ll ask the first question: "Walk me through a DCF you built — what are the main steps and the key assumptions you check?" Answer as you would in the room and I’ll score it and give one concrete fix.

Saved: nothing yet for Lincoln International. Is that right? (One question: do you want the 10‑minute mock now?)

You don't have any applications or a queued posting on file yet. The one step that starts this: pick a posting for me to prepare (paste the job link or say "prepare the first from search for [role] in [city]").

If you pick one, here is exactly what I will fill on the application card for that first posting — every field I will prepare or leave for you to confirm, in the order it will appear on the card. I assume a typical online form that asks for contact, resume, short message (if allowed), screening questions, attachments and availability. I will never submit anything without your approval in the extension.
1) Employer and role
- Company: exact company name from the posting.
- Job title: exact job title from the posting.
- Location: city / remote / on-site as the posting says.
- Link: the posting URL you gave (or the first result I fetched).

2) Resume selection
- Resume file to attach: I will list your confirmed resume files and show which one I plan to attach. If you have none confirmed, the card will show “[no confirmed resume — please upload or confirm]”.
- Resume contact line: name and email that will appear at the top of the resume (I will use the resume contact you saved; if none saved the card will ask for it).
3) Short cover note / message (when the posting accepts a message)
- Message draft (≤120 words): a tailored 100–120 word note that highlights 2–3 top matches between your experience and the posting’s key skills. Any missing specifics (hiring manager name, a particular project name, exact years) will be shown in brackets like [this].
- Where it goes: I will show whether this will be inserted into the employer's text field, an email body, or marked “not asked” if the posting does not accept a message.
4) Application form fields and screening questions
- Full list of required form fields the posting asks (e.g., “Are you authorized to work in X?”, “Years of experience in Y”, “Do you have X certification?”, “Salary expectations”).
- For each field I will either:
  - Pre-fill with a confirmed fact from your profile (exact wording shown), or
  - Leave as “[answer needed]” when you have not given a confirmed fact.
- For multi-choice or dropdowns I will select an answer only when a confirmed fact supports it; otherwise I leave it blank for you.
5) Attachments beyond resume
- Any additional requested attachments from the posting (portfolio, code sample, transcript, references). Each will show:
  - “Attached: [filename]” if you’ve confirmed it,
  - Or “[missing — attach to proceed]” if not available.

6) Additional text fields (cover letter upload, project descriptions)
- If the posting allows a full cover letter upload or project descriptions, I will draft them from your confirmed facts and the posting’s priorities and show the full text for your review with bracketed gaps.
7) Availability and start date
- Earliest start date: pre-filled from a confirmed fact or shown as “[start date?]”.
- Interview availability: left as “[provide availability]” unless you saved times.

8) Salary / compensation question
- If asked, I will fill salary only from a confirmed pay preference you set; otherwise I leave “[salary expectation?]”. I will not guess or invent numbers.

9) Work authorization / sponsorship
- Any question about authorization or sponsorship will be answered only from confirmed facts; otherwise left “[answer needed]”.
10) Short rationale / tailoring note for hiring manager
- A one- or two-line note explaining why you’re a fit (what I led with on the resume and the top achievements to highlight). This appears on the card as internal notes for you to edit.

11) Applicant-tracking tags and persona
- Role, seniority, location tags taken from the posting.
- Which resume persona is used (you choose from saved personas or I default to ‘base’); if you haven’t created personas, the card will show that and default.
12) Truth-check summary
- A clear list of every bracketed item that still needs your input (name/email if missing, authorization, start date, salary, missing attachments).
- A full preview: exactly how every field and text will appear on the employer’s form (resume filename, message text, each answered screening question).

13) What will and will not be sent automatically
- I will not press submit. Nothing is sent until you approve the card in the extension on your computer.
- I will not use any unconfirmed draft facts in application fields.
- I will not connect to your email or send follow-ups until you enable those features.
What you will see when I finish preparing the card
- An application card showing every field above, with exact text for each pre-filled answer and bracketed placeholders where your confirmation is needed.
- A one-line checklist of required actions you must complete on the card before I can queue it for sending (e.g., confirm resume, confirm authorization answer, attach portfolio).
- The exact next step wording: “Approve this card in the Trainee extension to queue or submit.”

One next step: paste the job link you want prepared (or say “prepare the first from search for [role] in [city]”) and I’ll fetch the posting and build the card exactly as described. Is that the one I should prepare?
